l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: The prologue explains how the Royal Historian of Oz resumed writing Oz stories after learning that Ozma of Oz had ordered Oz rendered invisible and communication with it cut off. Children suggested using wireless telegraphy to reach Princess Dorothy, so the Historian built a tower, learned wireless telegraphy, and sent wireless messages into the air. Glinda learned of the messages through her book of events, and a Shaggy Man in Oz sent a wireless reply, allowing Dorothy to obtain Ozma's permission to share the latest news. The volume is titled The Patchwork Girl of Oz and includes chapters about Ojo, the Patchwork Girl, and their adventures in Oz.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: This is the title of the book presented by the Royal Historian of Oz. The chapter list includes "The Patchwork Girl" as chapter 3.

l: Royal Historian of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: The Royal Historian was an American writer appointed through Dorothy Gale's kindness to chronicle the Land of Oz. After learning that Oz would become invisible and communication with it would end, he built a wireless tower, learned wireless telegraphy, and contacted Dorothy for new material.

l: Dorothy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: Dorothy Gale, afterward Princess Dorothy of Oz, helped the writer become Royal Historian of Oz. She learned through wireless communication that he wanted news from Oz and asked Ozma for permission to provide it.

l: Ozma, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: Ozma of Oz issued the edict that would render Oz invisible to those outside its borders and cut off future communication with the outside world. She graciously consented to Dorothy sharing the latest news of Oz with the Historian.

l: Glinda the Good, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: Glinda is described as a powerful Sorceress who possesses a book recording every event that takes place anywhere in the world as it happens. Through that book, she learned that the Historian was sending wireless messages and wanted to communicate with Dorothy.

l: children, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: Children who loved the Oz stories were disappointed when they believed no more books would be written. They sent letters asking for earlier adventures and suggested that Dorothy might communicate with the Historian by wireless telegraph.

l: Land of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: Oz is described as a wonderful and favored fairyland inhabited by gay and happy people. An edict was to make it invisible to outsiders and end its communication with the rest of the world.

l: Oz stories, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: The Royal Historian had written six books about the adventures of the people of Oz before communication with Oz was cut off. The children loved these stories, and another Oz story is presented after two years of waiting.

l: wireless telegraphy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: Wireless telegraphy provided a possible way to communicate with Dorothy without seeing her or knowing where Oz was. The Historian built a tower, took lessons, and learned enough to send messages.

l: wireless messages, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: The Historian sent wireless messages into the air calling for Princess Dorothy of Oz. Glinda learned about the messages, and a Shaggy Man in Oz sent a wireless reply.

l: edict rendering Oz invisible, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: The edict of Ozma of Oz declared that Oz would thereafter be invisible to everyone living outside its borders.

l: communication with Oz being cut off, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: The Royal Historian learned with sorrow that communication with Oz would be cut off after Oz was rendered invisible. This led him to seek another means of receiving news from Dorothy.

l: wireless communication with Dorothy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz / Prologue
s: Wireless communication with Dorothy was proposed by one of the children and made possible by the Historian's wireless equipment and a Shaggy Man in Oz who knew how to telegraph a wireless reply. It allowed the Historian to request the latest news of Oz after ordinary communication had ended.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: Ojo and his uncle, Unc Nunkie, live alone in a round house surrounded by woods in the Land of Oz. Their cupboard contains only bread, and the bread tree has just two unripe loaves left, so Ojo worries that they are poor and will soon have nothing to eat. Ojo suggests that they leave home to find food in the Munchkin Country, but Unc Nunkie thinks Ojo is too young. Unc Nunkie stays awake after Ojo falls asleep, silently considering the situation.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: Ojo is a Munchkin boy who lives alone with Unc Nunkie. He notices that their food is nearly gone, asks why they are poor, and urges Unc Nunkie to travel to the Munchkin Country to find food.

l: Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: Unc Nunkie is Ojo's old, long-bearded uncle, who speaks very few words and usually answers with brief statements. He objects that Ojo is too little to leave home and remains awake by the fire thinking after Ojo falls asleep.

l: Unc Nunkie's house, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: The house is a lonesome, round house where Ojo and Unc Nunkie have lived for as long as Ojo can remember. It has a little garden behind it and thick woods all around.

l: the bread tree, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: The bread tree is the only thing growing in Ojo and Unc Nunkie's yard. It has only two more loaves, and those loaves are not yet ripe.

l: bread, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: Bread is the only food in the cupboard, and Ojo eats the last ripe loaf while setting aside Unc Nunkie's share. The remaining loaves on the bread tree are not ripe yet.

l: food, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: There is no butter, jam, cake, jelly, apples, or other food in the house besides bread. Ojo says that food is plentiful in the Land of Oz, but they may need to go elsewhere to find it.

l: poverty, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: Ojo believes that he and Unc Nunkie are poor because they have only a house and bread, while other people in the Land of Oz have access to plenty. Unc Nunkie denies that they are poor but does not explain why.

l: leaving home to seek food, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter One
s: Ojo proposes that he and Unc Nunkie leave their house and visit the Munchkin Country because their food is running out. Unc Nunkie questions where they would go and says that Ojo is too little, so no departure occurs in this unit.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: At dawn, Ojo and Unc Nunkie leave their isolated home and travel through the Munchkin Country to visit Dr. Pipt, the Crooked Magician. Dame Margolotte welcomes them, feeds them, and explains Dr. Pipt's Powder of Life, which can bring objects to life. Dr. Pipt is nearly finished making a new batch of the powder for Margolotte, who has made a servant from her grandmother's old patchwork quilt. Margolotte brings the Patchwork Girl into the workshop to show Ojo and Unc Nunkie.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Ojo leaves his lonely forest home with Unc Nunkie because he wants to travel and see people. He learns that he is known as Ojo the Unlucky, meets Dr. Pipt and Dame Margolotte, and hears about the Powder of Life, the Glass Cat, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Patchwork Girl.

l: Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Unc Nunkie awakens Ojo, takes him from their home, and leads him up the mountain to Dr. Pipt's house. He reunites with his former friend Dr. Pipt and approves of Margolotte's plan for making the Patchwork Girl a servant.

l: Crooked Magician, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Dr. Pipt is the Crooked Magician who lives in a round blue house and is making the Powder of Life. He is so crooked that he stirs four kettles at once with his hands and feet, and he recognizes Unc Nunkie as the Silent One.

l: Margolotte, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Dame Margolotte welcomes Ojo and Unc Nunkie, gives them a meal, and explains Dr. Pipt's magic. She wants to use the new Powder of Life to bring her Patchwork Girl to life as a housework servant.

l: Land of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: The Land of Oz is the land where Ojo and Unc Nunkie live and travel. Princess Ozma rules it, and its regions favor different colors, with green popular at the Emerald City.

l: Munchkin Country, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: The Munchkin Country is part of the Land of Oz and is associated with the color blue. Ojo and Unc Nunkie travel from its remote forest through the mountains toward the Country of the Gillikins to reach Dr. Pipt's house.

l: the Magician's house, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Dr. Pipt's house is a large, round, blue house in a mountain clearing surrounded by forest. Its garden contains blue vegetables, flowers, bun-trees, cake-trees, cream-puff bushes, buttercups, and chocolate-caramel plants, while its workshop has a domed hall, windows, a fireplace, and four bubbling kettles.

l: Powder of Life, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: The Powder of Life is a magic substance that brings anything to life when sprinkled on it. Dr. Pipt previously gave a supply to Mombi the Witch in exchange for a Powder of Perpetual Youth that did not work, and Mombi used the Powder of Life to bring Jack Pumpkinhead to life.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: The Glass Cat was brought to life with the first batch of Dr. Pipt's Powder of Life and has lived ever since. She has pink brains, a blood-red stone heart, admires herself, and refuses to catch mice.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: The Patchwork Girl is a girl-shaped figure that Dame Margolotte made from her grandmother's many-colored patchwork quilt and stuffed with cotton-wadding. Margolotte intends for Dr. Pipt to bring her to life as a servant.

l: the creation of the Powder of Life, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Dr. Pipt's process takes several years and involves preparing a compound in four kettles. He is nearly finished with the new batch, which he is making for Margolotte's purpose.

l: Ojo and Unc Nunkie's journey to Dr. Pipt's house, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Ojo and Unc Nunkie leave their home at dawn, follow a path from the Munchkin Country up a mountain, and eat their remaining bread along the way. After traveling all morning and part of the afternoon, they reach Dr. Pipt's house.

l: the Patchwork Girl's creation and awakening, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Two
s: Margolotte plans to bring the Patchwork Girl to life by having Dr. Pipt sprinkle the Powder of Life over her. This has not yet happened in the unit; the Patchwork Girl is only brought into the workshop and shown to Ojo and Unc Nunkie.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Margolotte prepares a patchwork servant girl, giving her a stuffed body, sewn features, and selected qualities for brains. Ojo secretly adds powder from every bottle on the Brain Furniture shelf, including Cleverness, before the Patchwork Girl is brought to life. Dr. Pipt completes the Powder of Life after nearly six years of work and locks it away until morning. While Ojo, Margolotte, Unc Nunkie, and Dr. Pipt talk about magic, a strange cat enters the house.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Ojo examines the Patchwork Girl and praises her mouth. He secretly adds powder from every bottle on the Brain Furniture shelf to the dish intended for her brains, then comforts himself with the thought that one cannot have too much cleverness.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: The Patchwork Girl is made from a patchwork quilt, stuffed with cotton, and dressed in a patchwork skirt and apron. She has red leather shoes, gold fingernails, yarn hair, silver button eyes, gold ears, pearl teeth, and a multicolored patched face. Margolotte places a mixture of brain powders inside her head, but she is not brought to life during this unit.

l: Margolotte, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Margolotte constructs the Patchwork Girl and plans to give her only the qualities suitable for a servant, especially Obedience, Amiability, and Truth. She places the selected brain powders inside the girl's head and helps Dr. Pipt remove the finished Powder of Life from the kettles.

l: Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Unc Nunkie objects when Margolotte says the Patchwork Girl should not have very good brains and suggests giving her a little Cleverness. He later sits with Ojo, Margolotte, and Dr. Pipt while they admire the Powder of Life and talk.

l: Dr. Pipt, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Dr. Pipt, the Crooked Magician, completes his Powder of Life after nearly six years of preparation and stores it in a locked drawer until the next morning. He explains that he is proud of his crooked body and describes his Liquid of Petrifaction, which turns objects to marble. He also says that he is permitted to make a servant girl for his wife but is forbidden to work magic for others or as a profession.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: The cat scratches at the back door and asks to be let in. After giving the requested cat sound, it enters the room and stops when it sees the strangers, who stare at its unusual appearance.

l: the Land of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: The Land of Oz is described as a place where gold is the most common metal and is used for many purposes because it is soft and pliable. Princess Ozma has stopped most magic there, leaving only Glinda the Good permitted to practice her arts without harm.

l: Powder of Life, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: The Powder of Life is made from the contents of four kettles that boil away, leaving a small amount of fine white powder. Dr. Pipt says he alone knows how to make it and that it is worth the price of a kingdom. He places it in a small gold bottle and locks it away until it is cool and can be used the next morning.

l: the Patchwork Girl's brains, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Margolotte initially selects Obedience, Amiability, and Truth for the Patchwork Girl's brains and considers adding a little Cleverness. Ojo secretly adds some powder from every labeled bottle on the Brain Furniture shelf, including qualities such as Judgment, Courage, Ingenuity, Learning, Poesy, and Self Reliance, before Margolotte adds Cleverness.

l: magic, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Magic is described as an interesting study that has caused trouble in the Land of Oz when practiced by wicked Witches. Princess Ozma has forbidden most magical work, allowing Glinda the Good to practice and permitting Dr. Pipt only limited magic for his own purposes, such as making a servant girl or a Glass Cat.

l: the creation of the Powder of Life, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Three
s: Dr. Pipt creates the Powder of Life by stirring four kettles for nearly six years. After the contents boil away, he and Margolotte collect the remaining grains, mix them in a golden dish, cool the powder, and place it in a locked gold bottle.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: Dr. Pipt introduces Ojo and Unc Nunkie to the Glass Cat, a transparent animal with jeweled features, a ruby heart, and unusually advanced brains. The Glass Cat complains about Dr. Pipt, Margolotte, and its existence, while Margolotte argues with it about the Patchwork Girl's appearance and intended role as a servant. Ojo worries that he secretly added extra qualities to the brains sewn into the Patchwork Girl, contrary to Margolotte's wishes. After breakfast, Dr. Pipt prepares to bring the Patchwork Girl to life and sprinkles the Powder of Life over her head and arms.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: The Glass Cat is made almost entirely of clear glass, with pink balls in its head, emerald eyes, a blood-red ruby heart, and a spun-glass tail. It is intelligent, sarcastic, proud of its appearance, and dissatisfied with Dr. Pipt's household; it also considers the Patchwork Girl ugly and says it cannot respect her.

l: Dr. Pipt, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: Dr. Pipt explains the Glass Cat's nature and says that his magic made it live, although he considers it useless and troublesome. He plans to bring the Patchwork Girl to life and later says he may replace the Glass Cat's brains with pebbles. After breakfast, he prepares the Powder of Life and sprinkles it over the Patchwork Girl.

l: Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: Unc Nunkie is introduced as a descendant of the former kings of the Munchkins. He has lived alone in the forest with Ojo, says little, and watches as Dr. Pipt prepares to awaken the Patchwork Girl.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: Ojo is identified as a boy who is small because he is young and is expected to grow larger with age. He is fascinated by the Glass Cat and eager to see the Patchwork Girl brought to life, but he becomes worried because he secretly added extra qualities to the brains sewn into her head.

l: Margolotte, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: Margolotte is Dr. Pipt's wife and an excellent cook who wants the Patchwork Girl to become her household servant. She prepared brains containing only the qualities she thinks a humble servant requires, and she intends for the Patchwork Girl to wash dishes, sweep, and dust the house.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: The Patchwork Girl lies limp and lifeless on a bench, made from a bundle of differently colored scraps. Margolotte intends her to be a servant, while the Glass Cat criticizes her appearance; Ojo has added extra qualities to the brains inside her head without telling Margolotte.

l: magic, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: Dr. Pipt says that his magic made the Glass Cat and gave it life, but could not make it grow. He distinguishes this from Nature's magic, which makes a boy grow larger with age, and says that bringing the Patchwork Girl to life is a feat possible in Oz but nowhere else.

l: Powder of Life, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: The Powder of Life is kept in a gold bottle inside Dr. Pipt's locked cabinet. He takes it out during the preparation to awaken the Patchwork Girl and sprinkles some of it directly onto her head and arms.

l: the Patchwork Girl's creation and awakening, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Four
s: The Patchwork Girl was assembled from scraps, fitted with brains, and left lying lifeless on a bench. Dr. Pipt prepares her awakening with music and the Powder of Life, then sprinkles the powder over her, but the text ends before describing whether she becomes alive.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The Liquid of Petrifaction is accidentally spilled on Margolotte and Unc Nunkie, turning both into marble statues, while the Powder of Life brings a phonograph to life. Dr. Pipt discovers that the Powder of Life is exhausted and identifies a compound that could restore the petrified pair. Ojo agrees to search Oz for the required ingredients, accompanied by the Patchwork Girl and Bungle. The three leave with food and charms so Ojo can try to save Unc Nunkie and Margolotte.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Ojo is devastated when Unc Nunkie is turned to marble and initially believes the accident may be his fault. He agrees to find the ingredients for the restoring compound and leaves at once with the Patchwork Girl and Bungle.

l: Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Unc Nunkie accidentally knocks a bottle from a shelf, causing the Liquid of Petrifaction to spill on him and Margolotte. He is turned into a cold, hard marble statue, and Ojo promises to try to save him.

l: Crooked Magician, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Dr. Pipt is horrified when the Liquid of Petrifaction turns Margolotte and Unc Nunkie to marble. He finds that the Powder of Life has been exhausted, begins preparing to make more, and gives Ojo the recipe for a different restoring compound.

l: Margolotte, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Margolotte is accidentally struck by the Liquid of Petrifaction and becomes a motionless marble statue. Dr. Pipt says that restoring her will also restore Unc Nunkie.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The Patchwork Girl is frightened by the accident but quickly recovers and takes delight in her unusual appearance. She suggests using the Powder of Life to restore the petrified pair, chooses the name Scraps, and joins Ojo's search for the needed ingredients.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Bungle, the Glass Cat, hides under the table during the accident and later mocks the Patchwork Girl and criticizes Dr. Pipt. She reveals that Dr. Pipt made her with an early batch of the Powder of Life and allows her to remain unbroken despite her brittle glass body; she joins Ojo and the Patchwork Girl.

l: Powder of Life, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The Powder of Life accidentally falls onto the phonograph and makes it alive. Dr. Pipt discovers that every remaining grain has been wasted on the phonograph, so he begins a process that will take six years to make another batch.

l: the Liquid of Petrifaction, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The Liquid of Petrifaction is accidentally knocked from its shelf and spills on Margolotte and Unc Nunkie. It works immediately, turning both of them into stiff marble statues.

l: magic charm, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Dr. Pipt says that a compound can destroy the spell of the Liquid of Petrifaction and restore Margolotte and Unc Nunkie instantly. Its ingredients include a six-leaved clover, the left wing of a yellow butterfly, water from a dark well, three hairs from a Woozy's tail, and a drop of oil from a live man's body.

l: the six-leaved clover, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: A six-leaved clover is required for the restoring compound. Dr. Pipt says it can be found in the green country around the Emerald City and is very scarce there.

l: yellow butterfly, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The left wing of a yellow butterfly is required for the restoring compound. Dr. Pipt says that yellow butterflies can be found in the yellow country of the Winkies, west of the Emerald City.

l: Dark Well, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The restoring compound requires a gill of water from a dark well. The well must receive no daylight, and the water must be placed in a gold bottle without light reaching it.

l: Woozy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Three hairs from the tip of a Woozy's tail are required for the restoring compound. Dr. Pipt has never seen a Woozy and cannot describe what kind of animal it is.

l: Unc Nunkie's transformation into a marble statue, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The marble transformation occurs when the Liquid of Petrifaction strikes Margolotte and Unc Nunkie. They become motionless, stiff, cold, and hard like marble statues.

l: the accident involving Margolotte and Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: The terrible accident begins when the Patchwork Girl knocks the Powder of Life from Dr. Pipt's hand, startling Unc Nunkie and Margolotte. Unc Nunkie's movement upsets the Liquid of Petrifaction, which falls on him and Margolotte, while the Powder of Life lands on the phonograph.

l: Ojo's search for the magical ingredients, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Five
s: Ojo's rescue mission is to collect the ingredients for Dr. Pipt's restoring compound and return as quickly as possible. He undertakes the journey to save Unc Nunkie and Margolotte, traveling with the Patchwork Girl and Bungle.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat leave the Magician’s house and travel through the forest toward the Emerald City and the Country of the Winkies. They meet a Munchkin woodchopper, who warns that unauthorized magic is against the law and that their journey will cross lonely regions, rivers, and dark forests. At night they enter a roadside house where an unseen voice offers them beds but commands them to keep quiet. When Scraps refuses, an unseen hand throws her outside, while Ojo falls asleep inside.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: Ojo travels with Scraps and the Glass Cat toward the Country of the Winkies to obtain the left wing of a yellow butterfly. He discovers that the Magician has given him enchanted bread and cheese that remain the same size when eaten, and he guides the group through the dark by tying a string to the Glass Cat. He enters the roadside house and falls asleep after Scraps is thrown outside.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: Scraps enjoys the forest and is pleased by her freedom, bright colors, and many brains. She cannot eat because she has no opening beyond her mouth, and she teases the Glass Cat while leaping over a brook. At the roadside house, she refuses to keep quiet and is seized by an unseen hand, thrown outside, and locked out.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The Glass Cat travels with Ojo and Scraps and says that her transparent body, red heart, and pink brains make her superior. She cannot eat and claims that her eyes are better than Ojo’s, allowing her to see in the dark. She leads the others to the roadside house but becomes afraid when she cannot find the owner of the voice.

l: the journey through the mountains, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The journey takes Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat from the forest toward the Emerald City and the Country of the Winkies. They are warned that the route includes lonely parts of Oz, rivers, and dark forests, and they spend the first night at a roadside house.

l: the Land of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The Land of Oz contains Munchkin Country, the Emerald City, and the Country of the Winkies. Magic may legally be practiced only by Glinda the Good and the royal Wizard of Oz, according to the woodchopper.

l: Munchkin Country, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: Munchkin Country lies beyond the mountainside forest and has broad blue fields and many blue-domed houses. Its people have pale, colorless skins and blue clothing.

l: the Blue Forest, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The forest lies along the path from the mountainside into Munchkin Country. Ojo finds it gloomy and sad, while Scraps admires its trees, ferns, wildflowers, and mosses. The travelers leave it near sundown and later pass through darkness beyond its edge.

l: the path, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The path initially leads through the forest and is the only route available to the travelers. It becomes broader and more distinct after they leave the woodchopper, but grows difficult for Ojo and Scraps to see after nightfall.

l: the woodchopper, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The woodchopper lives alone in a small leaf-covered house at the edge of the forest. He laughs at Scraps, warns that the Magician’s creations may be arrested near the Emerald City, and explains that unauthorized magic is illegal. He tells them about Dorothy and the Tin Woodman and warns that their route to the Winkies will be long and dangerous before inviting them to stay the night.

l: the roadside house, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The roadside house is dark and silent, with three prepared beds. Its unseen occupant allows Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat to enter only if they make no noise and go directly to bed. Scraps is thrown out when she refuses to keep quiet, and the door is locked behind her.

l: Emerald City, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The Emerald City is the destination toward which the travelers are heading. The woodchopper warns that they could be arrested if they go near it because the Magician’s magic is unlawful.

l: the yellow butterfly's left wing, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The yellow butterfly's left wing is the object Ojo and his companions intend to obtain in the Country of the Winkies.

l: the unseen voice, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Six
s: The unseen voice speaks from inside the roadside house and permits the travelers to enter for the night. It repeatedly orders them to make no noise and go to bed, but its owner cannot be seen even by the Glass Cat.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: Ojo wakes in a Munchkin house, eats breakfast, and continues traveling with the Glass Cat and Patchwork Girl. They are joined by a living phonograph that has run away from Dr. Pipt after quarreling with him. The phonograph plays classical music and rag-time, but the travelers find both unbearable and send it away. Ojo, the Glass Cat, and Patchwork Girl then continue along the widest path toward the Emerald City.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: Ojo wakes in a Munchkin house, washes, eats the breakfast left for him, and leaves with the Glass Cat. He objects to the phonograph joining the party, threatens to smash its record when it will not stop playing, and decides to continue straight ahead toward the Emerald City.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: The Glass Cat sleeps in the Munchkin house and then travels with Ojo and Patchwork Girl. It criticizes the phonograph's squeaky, noisy machinery and says that both its classical music and rag-time are unbearable.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: Patchwork Girl spends the night outside watching the stars, the moon, and a gray wolf. She welcomes the phonograph, calls it Vic, asks it to play music, and then helps drive it away after finding both of its records unpleasant.

l: Phonograph, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: The phonograph, brought to life by the Crooked Magician's Powder of Life, runs away from Dr. Pipt after their quarrel. It catches up with Ojo, the Glass Cat, and Patchwork Girl, plays classical music and rag-time, and is sent toward a distant Munchkin village because the travelers consider it a nuisance.

l: Victor Columbia Edison, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: Victor Columbia Edison is the name the phonograph gives when Patchwork Girl asks what it is called. Patchwork Girl shortens the name to Vic.

l: classical music, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: The phonograph describes classical music as highly puzzling music that people are supposed to like. When it plays its classical record, Ojo covers his ears, the Glass Cat snarls, and Patchwork Girl laughs before they make the phonograph stop.

l: rag-time, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: The phonograph says rag-time is the opposite of classical music and plays it after Patchwork Girl turns over the record. The jerky jumble of sounds confuses the travelers, and Patchwork Girl stops it by stuffing her apron into the horn.

l: music, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: The phonograph claims that it is meant to talk, make noise, and sometimes play music. Ojo, the Glass Cat, and Patchwork Girl cannot appreciate the music it produces and regard it as a nuisance.

l: phonograph's escape, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: The phonograph escapes from Dr. Pipt's house while the Magician is stirring his four kettles. It runs after Ojo and his companions throughout the night because it wants pleasant company and freedom to talk and play tunes.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Seven
s: After leaving the Munchkin house, Ojo, the Glass Cat, and Patchwork Girl continue their journey. Ojo chooses the widest and best path and plans to ask for directions to the Emerald City when they reach a house.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: Ojo, Scraps, and the other travelers stop at the Foolish Owl and Wise Donkey's house to seek advice. The Wise Donkey explains that the Foolish Owl is extremely foolish but says her poems contain advice, while he gives directions to the Emerald City. Ojo learns to follow their path until it reaches the yellow brick road, which leads directly to the Emerald City. The travelers accept the advice to move on and resume their journey.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: Ojo visits the Wise Donkey and Foolish Owl's house with the other travelers. He asks how to reach the Emerald City and learns that he should follow the path until it reaches the yellow brick road.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: Scraps suggests entering the house of the Foolish Owl and Wise Donkey to get advice. She compares the Foolish Owl's poem with her own poetry and later recognizes the owl's final poem as a hint to continue traveling.

l: the Wise Donkey, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The Wise Donkey welcomes the travelers and offers advice. He says the yellow brick road leads directly to the Emerald City and advises the travelers to keep following their path and move on. He explains that he was born in the Land of Mo and has remained in the Land of Oz since it was shut off from the rest of the world.

l: the Foolish Owl, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The Foolish Owl sits on a shelf wearing a blue sunbonnet and speaks in rhyming, nonsensical verses. Her poems describe Scraps, Ojo's search for a charm, and the travelers' uncertain journey. The Wise Donkey says she is extremely foolish but admires her for being unusual.

l: Emerald City, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The Emerald City is the travelers' destination. The Wise Donkey says that the yellow brick road leads directly to it.

l: the road of yellow bricks, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The yellow brick road is reached by continuing along the path the travelers are following. The Wise Donkey says it is the only yellow thing in the blue country and that it leads directly to the Emerald City.

l: the Foolish Owl and Wise Donkey's house, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The house stands beside the roadside and bears a sign identifying the Foolish Owl and Wise Donkey as public advisers. Inside, the Wise Donkey dusts the furniture while the Foolish Owl sits on a shelf.

l: advice, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The Wise Donkey says advice is free unless it is followed. He advises the travelers to follow their current path to the yellow brick road and to move on so they will reach the Emerald City sooner.

l: magic charm, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The Foolish Owl's poem says that Ojo is searching for a charm and that charms are scarce and hard to get.

l: the journey through the mountains, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eight
s: The travelers stop at the Foolish Owl and Wise Donkey's house during their journey. After receiving directions and hearing the owl's final hint, they say goodbye and resume traveling toward the Emerald City.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat enter the Woozy's fenced forest to obtain three hairs from the end of the Woozy's tail for the Crooked Magician's magic charm. The Woozy agrees to help after Ojo feeds it bread and cheese, but its three hairs cannot be pulled out. Scraps discovers that the Woozy's eye fire can burn through the fence when the group makes it angry by shouting "Krizzle-Kroo!" The Woozy escapes with them after promising not to eat honey-bees, and they continue seeking the road of yellow bricks and the other things Ojo needs.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Ojo travels with Scraps and the Glass Cat while seeking the road of yellow bricks and items needed to save Unc Nunkie and Margolotte. He enters the Woozy's forest, feeds the Woozy bread and cheese, and asks for its three tail hairs, but cannot pull them out. He then agrees to take the Woozy to the Crooked Magician so the hairs can be removed there.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Scraps climbs over the fence into the Woozy's forest and encourages Ojo to face the Woozy. She helps Ojo try to pull out one of the Woozy's tail hairs and later realizes that the Woozy can escape by using its eye fire to burn the fence. She joins Ojo and the Glass Cat in shouting "Krizzle-Kroo!" and continues traveling with the Woozy.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Glass Cat enters the Woozy's forest by creeping between the lower bars of the fence. It warns that the Woozy's hairs cannot be pulled out and questions how the Woozy will escape. It joins the others in shouting "Krizzle-Kroo!" to make the Woozy angry.

l: Woozy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Woozy is a dark blue, square-shaped creature with no hair except three stiff hairs at the extreme end of its tail. It has a thick skin that cannot be pierced, can run swiftly and jump high, but cannot climb, dig, or gnaw. After eating Ojo's bread and cheese, it agrees to give Ojo its three tail hairs, but the hairs will not come out, so it escapes from its forest with Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat.

l: Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Unc Nunkie is one of the people Ojo is trying to restore to life after an accident. The Crooked Magician requires the Woozy's three tail hairs as part of the magic charm intended to restore him.

l: Margolotte, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Margolotte is one of the people Ojo is trying to restore to life after an accident. The Crooked Magician requires the Woozy's three tail hairs as part of the magic charm intended to restore her.

l: Crooked Magician, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Crooked Magician has sent Ojo to obtain three hairs from the end of a Woozy's tail. Ojo believes the Crooked Magician may be able to remove the hairs if he brings the Woozy to the magician's house.

l: Munchkin farmers, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Munchkin farmers kept honey-bees to make honey and tried to destroy the Woozy because it ate their bees. When they could not hurt it, they drove it into a forest and built a fence around it.

l: the road of yellow bricks, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Ojo and his companions are seeking the road of yellow bricks while traveling through the dismal blue country. They have not yet found it in this unit.

l: forest (Woozy's forest), The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Woozy's forest is enclosed by a high fence and contains tall, closely set trees and a rocky cave where the Woozy lives. Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat enter it and later leave with the Woozy through an opening burned in the fence.

l: fence around Woozy's forest, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Munchkin farmers built the high fence around the Woozy's forest to imprison the creature because it ate their honey-bees. The fence is too tall for the Woozy to climb or jump over, but the Woozy's eye fire burns through one of its boards and creates an opening.

l: three hairs from a Woozy's tail, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Woozy's three tail hairs are its only hairs and its sole ornaments. Ojo needs them for the Crooked Magician's magic charm, but neither Ojo nor Scraps can pull even one out, so Ojo plans to bring the Woozy to the magician.

l: magic charm, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The magic charm is intended to help restore Unc Nunkie and Margolotte to life. The Woozy's three tail hairs are one part of the charm.

l: Unc Nunkie and Margolotte's restoration to life, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Ojo and his companions are seeking materials for the restoration of Unc Nunkie and Margolotte to life. Ojo fears that without the Woozy's three tail hairs, the other things he finds will be useless.

l: the accident involving Margolotte and Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: Ojo tells the Woozy that an accident caused Unc Nunkie and Margolotte's condition and that the three tail hairs are needed to help restore them to life.

l: Woozy's imprisonment, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Munchkin farmers imprisoned the Woozy in a fenced forest after failing to destroy it. The Woozy says it has lived there for years without food because there are no honey-bees and the leaves, mosses, and vines do not suit its taste.

l: Woozy's escape, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Woozy escapes its fenced forest after its eyes flash fire and burn through a fence board. It leaves with Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat after promising not to eat honey-bees while traveling with them.

l: honey-bees, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Woozy enjoys eating honey-bees and had eaten the bees kept by the Munchkin farmers for honey. Ojo makes the Woozy promise not to eat any honey-bees while it travels with their group.

l: Krizzle-Kroo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: "Krizzle-Kroo" is a phrase that makes the Woozy terribly angry, although the Woozy does not know what it means. Ojo, Scraps, and the Glass Cat shout it together, causing the Woozy's eyes to flash fire and burn the fence.

l: Woozy's eye fire, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Nine
s: The Woozy's eyes flash real fire when it becomes very angry. The eye fire burns the wooden fence after the group shouts "Krizzle-Kroo!," allowing the Woozy to escape.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: Ojo and his companions reach the yellow brick road and head west toward the Emerald City. They are captured by monstrous plants whose leaves fold around them, leaving Ojo despairing that no one can save them. The Shaggy Man arrives, uses whistling to control the plants, and cuts Ojo and his companions free. He introduces himself to Ojo and rescues Scraps, the Glass Cat, and the Woozy.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: Ojo travels with Scraps, the Glass Cat, the Woozy, and Bungle toward the Emerald City. A monstrous plant captures him and holds him inside a folded leaf until the Shaggy Man cuts him free. Ojo then asks the Shaggy Man to rescue his companions.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: Scraps worries that the colors of her patches might fade. A monstrous plant captures her, but the Shaggy Man cuts down the leaf and releases her; she immediately likes him after he laughs and calls her a wonder.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The Glass Cat fears being damaged because she is brittle. A monstrous plant rolls her inside a leaf, but the Shaggy Man cuts the leaf down and rescues her.

l: Woozy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The Woozy directs the travelers west on the yellow brick road and warns them to run when the monstrous plants attack. A plant captures him, but the Shaggy Man cuts down the leaf and the Woozy escapes.

l: Shaggy Man, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The Shaggy Man is a large, shaggy man with kindly blue eyes, a jeweled green velvet hat, and a sharp knife. He rescues Ojo and his companions from the monstrous plants by cutting down the leaves, and he says he must introduce Scraps to the Scarecrow.

l: Emerald City, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The Emerald City is the travelers' destination, and the Woozy says they should follow the yellow brick road west to reach it. Ojo has heard from Unc Nunkie that Ozma, the girl Ruler, is kind and helps those in trouble.

l: the road of yellow bricks, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The yellow brick road is broad and winding, with smooth, bright yellow bricks that follow the easiest route over hills and dales. Ojo and his companions find it and travel west toward the Emerald City.

l: monstrous plants, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The monstrous plants grow in rows along both sides of the yellow brick road and have tall, broad leaves that continually sway without wind. Their leaves display changing colors and can bend down to seize and imprison travelers.

l: capture by the monstrous plants, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The monstrous plants capture Scraps, the Glass Cat, the Woozy, and Ojo by folding their leaves around them. The captives are held in darkness and cannot escape until the Shaggy Man intervenes.

l: Shaggy Man's rescue, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The Shaggy Man rescues Ojo by cutting down the leaf that holds him. He then cuts down the leaves holding Scraps, the Glass Cat, and the Woozy, freeing all of Ojo's companions.

l: whistling that charms the plants, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Ten
s: The Shaggy Man's whistling makes the monstrous plants straighten and remain still. He explains that singing or whistling charms them and is the only way to make them behave.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The Shaggy Man joins Ojo, Scraps, the Glass Cat, and the Woozy on their journey toward the Emerald City to help them find the things required by the Crooked Magician to restore Unc Nunkie and Margolotte. He explains that a six-leaved clover may be found near the Emerald City, while a yellow butterfly, a dark well, and a drop of oil from a live man's body may be difficult to find. The travelers encounter the damaged live phonograph, whose song irritates the Shaggy Man and causes it to flee. That night, the group shelters in a deserted cabin, where the Shaggy Man sings about the Land of Oz and its unusual inhabitants.

l: Shaggy Man, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The Shaggy Man meets Ojo, Scraps, the Glass Cat, and the Woozy, listens to Ojo's quest, and tries unsuccessfully to pull three hairs from the Woozy's tail. He agrees to accompany the group to the Emerald City and introduce them to his friends, including the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow. He sings a song about the Land of Oz at the travelers' overnight shelter.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: Ojo tells the Shaggy Man about the Crooked Magician's requirements and his attempt to save Unc Nunkie and Margolotte. He continues traveling toward the Emerald City, shares bread and cheese with the Woozy, and asks the Shaggy Man for a story.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: Scraps jokes with the Shaggy Man, rejects dignity, and urges the group to reach the Emerald City quickly. She is entertained by the Shaggy Man's song and later carefully considers his advice to make friends with Eureka.

l: Glass Cat, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The Glass Cat jokes that its pink brains can be seen working and compares itself with the Scarecrow. It asks whether Dorothy's Pink Kitten is as pretty as it is and learns that making friends with Eureka could help it at the royal palace.

l: Woozy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The Woozy allows the Shaggy Man to try to pull hairs from its tail, but the hairs cannot be removed. It dislikes the Shaggy Man's condensed meal because it wants food it can chew and taste, so Ojo gives it bread and cheese.

l: Victor Columbia Edison, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The live phonograph returns with its wooden case marred, dented, and scratched after having objects thrown at it. It plays the popular song 'My Lulu,' angering the Shaggy Man, and then runs away before he can take it apart.

l: Land of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The Land of Oz is described as a fine fairyland with a pleasant country and climate, where magic is treated as ordinary. The Shaggy Man's song names many of its unusual inhabitants and rulers.

l: Emerald City, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The Emerald City is the travelers' next destination because a six-leaved clover may be found there. The Shaggy Man says it is still several days away and offers to guide the group there.

l: Crooked Magician, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The Crooked Magician requires five things for a charm that can restore the marble figures to life: three hairs from a Woozy's tail, a six-leaved clover, the left wing of a yellow butterfly, a gill of water from a dark well, and a drop of oil from a live man's body.

l: Unc Nunkie, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: Unc Nunkie was terribly injured in the accident at the Crooked Magician's house and has been turned into a marble figure. Ojo is searching for the Crooked Magician's required things to help restore him to life.

l: Margolotte, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: Margolotte was involved in the terrible accident at the Crooked Magician's house and was turned into a marble figure. Ojo's quest is also intended to restore her to life.

l: the six-leaved clover, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The six-leaved clover is one of the five things required by the Crooked Magician. The Shaggy Man says it may be found in the fields around the Emerald City, although a law forbids picking it.

l: yellow butterfly, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The left wing of a yellow butterfly is one of the five things required by the Crooked Magician. The Shaggy Man directs Ojo toward the Winkie Country, the yellow country of Oz, although he has never noticed butterflies there.

l: Dark Well, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: A gill of water from a dark well is one of the five things required by the Crooked Magician. Neither Ojo nor the Shaggy Man knows where such a well can be found, so the Shaggy Man suggests asking the Scarecrow.

l: drop of oil from a live man's body, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: A drop of oil from a live man's body is one of the five things required by the Crooked Magician. The Shaggy Man doubts that such oil exists, but Ojo continues searching because the Crooked Magician said the recipe would not require something that could not be found.

l: five things required by the Crooked Magician, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Eleven
s: The five things required by the Crooked Magician are three hairs from a Woozy's tail, a six-leaved clover, the left wing of a yellow butterfly, a gill of water from a dark well, and a drop of oil from a live man's body. Ojo and his companions continue toward the Emerald City while searching for them.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: Ojo and his companions travel toward the Emerald City and must walk backward to cross a section of the road of yellow bricks that slides them backward. They encounter Chiss, a giant porcupine whose quills can be thrown in any direction, and the Woozy's attempted growl fails to frighten him. Chiss attacks with a shower of quills, injuring the Shaggy Man and Scraps, but the travelers collect all of Chiss's quills and leave him harmless. Ojo uses a charm for flesh wounds to heal the Shaggy Man's leg before they continue their journey.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: Ojo travels with the Shaggy Man, Scraps, the Woozy, and the Glass Cat toward the Emerald City while seeking what is needed to restore Unc Nunkie. He notices the road's backward-sliding trick, helps collect Chiss's quills, and uses a flesh-wound charm to heal the Shaggy Man's injured leg.

l: Shaggy Man, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: The Shaggy Man recognizes the road's backward-sliding trick and teaches the others to walk backward to cross it. He is struck in the leg during Chiss's quill attack, captures Chiss, and forces the porcupine to remain harmless by having the others collect all its quills.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: Scraps travels with Ojo and the others and follows the Shaggy Man's instructions to cross the sliding road. She shields Ojo during Chiss's quill attack, becoming covered with quills, then helps gather them; the quills leave holes in her patches that the flesh-wound charm cannot repair.

l: Woozy, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: The Woozy claims that its growl is tremendously frightening and tries to scare Chiss, but it produces only a small squeak. It is not injured by Chiss's quill attack because its skin is thick and tough, and it admits that it may have been mistaken about the power of its growl.

l: Chiss, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: Chiss is a giant porcupine regarded in Oz as an evil spirit because it can throw its quills in any direction. After attacking the travelers, it is held prisoner by the Shaggy Man while Ojo and Scraps collect all its quills, leaving it unable to hurt anyone.

l: the road of yellow bricks, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: The road of yellow bricks leads Ojo and his companions toward the Emerald City. In one section, the surrounding landscape and the road move backward while the yellow bricks remain still, requiring the travelers to walk backward before they can continue forward.

l: the road's backward-sliding trick, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: The road's backward-sliding trick carries anyone walking upon that section back toward where they started. The Shaggy Man knows that walking backward lets travelers gain ground and pass safely beyond the troublesome section.

l: Chiss's quill attack, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Twelve
s: Chiss's quill attack sends a shower of quills toward the travelers when they come too near. Scraps shields Ojo and is pierced by many quills, the Shaggy Man is wounded in the leg, and the Glass Cat and the Woozy remain unharmed.

l: The Patchwork Girl of Oz, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Thirteen
s: Scraps, Ojo, the Shaggy Man, the Woozy, and the Glass Cat pass through an optical-illusion wall and continue toward the Emerald City. Ojo searches for a six-leaved clover despite being warned that picking one violates Ozma's law, then agrees to avoid the clover. They meet the Scarecrow of Oz riding the Sawhorse, and Ojo explains that the Woozy's three tail hairs are needed to restore Unc Nunkie from a marble statue. The Scarecrow advises Ojo to seek Dorothy's help because Ozma may not permit the Crooked Magician's restoration magic, and he leaves for a visit with Jinjur before planning to return to the Emerald City.

l: Scraps, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Thirteen
s: Scraps helps the travelers pass through the wall by following Ojo with her hands on his shoulders, although she cannot close her button eyes. A farmhouse woman repairs the holes in her body, and Scraps refuses an offer to stay for a new hat. She meets the Scarecrow of Oz, exchanges compliments with him, and attracts his enthusiastic admiration.

l: Ojo, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Thirteen
s: Ojo travels with the others through the optical-illusion barrier toward the Emerald City. He searches for a six-leaved clover despite the Shaggy Man's warning that picking one violates Ozma's law, but eventually returns to the road. He tells the Scarecrow of Oz about Unc Nunkie's transformation and insists that he will restore his uncle with or without Ozma's permission.

l: Shaggy Man, The Patchwork Girl of Oz, Chapter Thirteen
s: The Shaggy Man leads the travelers through the apparent wall by having them close their eyes and walk forward. He explains that the wall is an optical illusion and warns Ojo to obey Ozma's law concerning six-leaved clovers. He introduces the travelers to the Scarecrow of Oz and advises Ojo about the danger of displeasing Ozma.
